open-question.question: What happens to the dated hands-on check block heading each of the three scripts/hosts/<host>/settings.toml files? Each block is the one record of that host's hands-on check, naming the date, the installed version checked, and what the run covered, and it quotes install commands, invocations, agent names, and cache paths under the old name; a later re-check is what updates a block. Not settled is whether the rename runs a fresh hands-on check on each host under the new name and rewrites the block from it, rewrites only the quoted names with no new check, or leaves each block as the record of the check that was run.
open-question.recommendation: A host suite run under the new name is a re-check in the form the blocks already record, so it enters each block as one dated sentence with the bullets it covered rewritten from it, which puts the rename's name-dependent surface on record as checked on every host. The earlier dated sentences stay true to the runs they describe, where a substitution would claim commands that never ran.
open-question.alternative: Each host gets a re-check of the name-dependent points only (install under the new marketplace and plugin id, the `gurita:` namespace or invocation form, agent dispatch by the new names, the install and cache paths), taken from a host suite run against the renamed installed copy in the form the 2026-11-09 re-checks already used; a dated "Re-checked" sentence naming that run and the installed version is added, the bullets it covered (Install, Dispatch, and the paths) are rewritten from it, and the earlier dated sentences and the bullets it did not cover stay as written, carried forward under their original names. Records the rename's riskiest surface, which no drift gate or test run touches, as actually checked on each host, in the block's own established update form, while leaving every older statement true. Needs a host suite run on all three hosts against renamed installed copies whose result can still be committed as a block update, so it depends on the sibling questions on host suite timing and on how the installed copies come to equal the build (a run only at the release pre-flight could not land in the release commit, which may change only version slots); the older dated sentences keep the old name, so the completeness bar must allow them.

No new hands-on check is run and no line of the three dated blocks is edited: each block stays exactly as written, old-name install commands, invocations (`/cairn:answer-all-open-questions-with-recommendation`, `codex plugin add cairn@cairn`), agent names (`cairn:`-namespaced), and paths (`~/.gemini/config/plugins/cairn`, `~/.codex/plugins/cache/cairn/cairn/`) included, as the record of the checks that ran. The blocks change only when a later re-check, made for its own reasons, updates them in the usual way. Keeps each block a true record of what was run, against which installed version, under which name, and follows the convention that only a re-check updates a block; it costs nothing. The blocks then quote commands and paths that no longer work and contradict the settings beside them (the Antigravity block calls `~/.gemini/config/plugins/cairn` "the plugin_root path below" while plugin_root reads gurita), and none of the rename's name-dependent surface is recorded as hands-on checked; the three blocks also become standing old-name residue, which depends on the completeness bar owned by the rename-completeness question listing them as allowed.

No new hands-on check is run; every occurrence of the old name in the three blocks (commands, invocations, namespaced agent names, install and cache paths) is replaced by its new form, and the dates, installed versions, and observations stay as written. This is what the milestone-to-mission rename did to the Claude Code block's one occurrence of the old word. Leaves no old name in scripts/hosts/ and keeps every block consistent with the settings and slot values beside it, at the cost of a plain substitution, with precedent in the word's rename. Each block would then state that commands such as `/gurita:…` and `codex plugin add gurita@gurita` ran on dates and versions when they did not, so the one record of each host's check claims a check of exactly the surface the rename changes and nothing exercised; unlike the word's rename, which changed prose, these are the identifiers a host resolves.

No new hands-on check is run; the existing text of each block stays verbatim, and one short dated sentence is added to each block saying that the check it records ran under the former name and stating how the quoted identifiers map to the new ones (namespace, plugin id, install and cache paths), with no claim that anything was re-checked. Keeps the record true while removing the apparent contradiction with the renamed settings, so a reader of the block knows the quoted commands are the pre-rename forms and what they are now, without the cost of a check. Adds to the block a line that records no check, departing from the rule that only a re-check updates it, and still leaves the name-dependent surface hands-on unchecked and the old name standing in the blocks, so it too depends on the rename-completeness question's bar allowing those occurrences.

Each host gets the same narrow re-check of the name-dependent points from a host suite run under the new name, recorded as a dated "Re-checked" sentence with the covered bullets rewritten from it, and in addition every remaining old-name occurrence in the block, in earlier dated sentences and carried-forward bullets alike, is replaced by its new form. Leaves no old name anywhere in scripts/hosts/ while the identifiers that matter most are backed by a real check under the new name, so the blocks need no allowance in the completeness bar. The rewritten earlier sentences (the 2026-11-09 `codex plugin add cairn@cairn` install, the 2026-10-18 `/cairn:` run) would claim forms those runs never used, falsifying the part of the record the new check did not cover; it carries the same dependence on the host suite timing and installed-copy sibling questions.

Each host gets a complete fresh hands-on check under the new name, covering every point its current block records (install, invocation, dispatch, waiting, continuing an agent, the context file, and the slot values each block sourced or confirmed), and each block is rewritten whole from that run, replacing the old one with nothing carried forward under the old name. Every block ends wholly current and wholly true, naming the new identifiers, the installed versions now on the machine, and observations made under the name the plugin now has. By far the largest cost: three hosts' worth of headless and provoked-failure runs re-sourcing slot values the rename does not touch, work outside a goal that is a rename, and it can contradict slot values and so widen the mission; it likewise needs renamed installed copies on all three hosts, which depends on the installed-copy and host suite timing sibling questions.

open-question.question: Who makes the changes on GitHub that the release depends on, a task of this mission through gh or the maintainer by hand: renaming the source repository to uHappyLogic/gurita, bringing the three distribution repositories to their new names, updating their descriptions and topics, and confirming that the one fine-grained TRAFFIC_TOKEN still covers all four repositories under their new names? The release procedure only checks that each distribution repository exists and holds the token, and treats provisioning a repository as the maintainer's own act, printing the commands and never running them.
open-question.recommendation: Renaming and provisioning public repositories is the act the release procedure reserves for the maintainer, and its pre-flight check, under the new names, already gates the release on each distribution repository and its secret and prints the creation and token steps. A missed source rename stops the publish at a point a re-run resumes from, so the mission needs no task of its own for a one-time act.
open-question.alternative: The maintainer makes every change by hand, outside the task list, at any time before the release: renaming the source repository, the distribution-repository transition, descriptions and topics, the local origin URL, and any extension, regeneration, and re-setting of TRAFFIC_TOKEN. No task of this mission records or checks the changes. The release pre-flight's existing check, with only its repository names changed to the new form, is the one gate, and it prints commands for a missing repository without running them, as it does now. It keeps the division the release procedure already draws, with provisioning as the maintainer's deliberate act, and no agent touches public GitHub state. The mission adds no task or check for a one-time act. The pre-flight checks only that each distribution repository exists and holds a secret named TRAFFIC_TOKEN. It checks neither the source repository's rename, nor descriptions and topics, nor whether the token still covers the renamed repositories, so a miss shows up at release time with every rename task done, or later as a failing badge workflow. Nothing in the mission's record shows the changes were made. The commands the check prints create fresh repositories, which fits only one outcome of the transition decision.

A task of this mission, placed before the release task, makes every GitHub-side change through gh: it renames the source repository to uHappyLogic/gurita, brings the three distribution repositories to uHappyLogic/gurita-<host> in whatever way the transition decision settles, sets each repository's description and topics to the new name, and points the checkout's origin at the new URL. It then confirms the token by running each of the four repositories' traffic-badges workflow once and checking that every run succeeds, stopping with the maintainer's web-settings steps for any repository whose run fails. The maintainer does nothing by hand unless that check fails. Every change and its proof land in one Task-completion commit with a verified bar, before the release task runs, so nothing the release depends on is left to the maintainer's memory and a missing piece is found ahead of the release rather than at its pre-flight. An agent, possibly in an unattended run, makes public and partly irreversible changes that the release procedure explicitly reserves for the maintainer, under whatever admin rights the machine's gh login carries. The token's repository access can be edited only in GitHub's web settings, so where the transition decision creates repositories fresh, the token step falls back to the maintainer in any case and the task stops mid-run.

The maintainer makes every change by hand, as in the no-task course. A task of this mission, placed before the release task, then checks the result through gh. Its read-only calls confirm that all four repositories stand under their new names with the new description and topics, that each holds TRAFFIC_TOKEN, and that the checkout's origin points at uHappyLogic/gurita. It runs each repository's traffic-badges workflow once and requires every run to succeed, which is what confirms that the token still covers the repository under its new name. The task changes no repository setting itself. The public and irreversible acts stay with the maintainer, where the release procedure puts them, while the result is checked against the whole list (token coverage included) and recorded in a verified bar before the release task starts. The task cannot pass until the maintainer has acted, so a run through the task list stops there, with a FAILED return in an unattended run, and the maintainer's part sits outside any record. The workflow runs are writes by an agent, each pushing to a traffic-data branch, though only the push the daily schedule already makes.

The work is divided by reach and reversibility. A task of this mission makes the changes gh can make and a later rename can undo: the source repository's rename, renaming the distribution repositories where the transition decision renames them, descriptions, topics, and the checkout's origin URL. The maintainer does what gh cannot do or what cannot be undone: creating any fresh repository, keeping, archiving, or deleting an old one, editing the fine-grained token's repository access in the web settings, and regenerating and re-setting the secret. A task then confirms the whole result, running each repository's traffic-badges workflow once. The mechanical bulk is automated and recorded, and the only acts left to a person are the ones gh cannot perform or that cannot be taken back, so the reserved provisioning stays the maintainer's. Two actors take turns, so the task list has to stop for the maintainer between the agent's part and the check, and the line between the parts depends on the transition decision. Where the repositories are renamed in place, little or nothing is left for the maintainer and this course comes close to the task acting alone. Where they are created fresh, most of the work is the maintainer's.

The maintainer makes every change by hand, and no task of this mission performs or checks them. Instead, the rename of /release-plugin widens its pre-flight check. Beyond each distribution repository's existence and its TRAFFIC_TOKEN secret, the check also confirms that the source repository stands at uHappyLogic/gurita and that each repository carries the description and topics the skill's provisioning commands name. On any mismatch it prints the commands for the maintainer, as it does for a missing repository, and stops before anything is published. The check outlives this mission: every later release verifies the same GitHub-side state, and the provisioning stance stays exactly as the release procedure states it, with no agent making a public change. A shortfall is still first seen at the release, after every rename task is done. The pre-flight cannot confirm that the token covers a renamed repository without running a workflow, which the skill does not do, and it gains permanent checks of descriptions and topics for what is mostly a one-time change. How much that stop costs depends on who runs the release, which a sibling question settles.

open-question.question: How should the next release treat this mission's finish, which lands after the release it publishes? The release is the mission's last task, so its Mission-finish commit comes after the release's tag, and the release procedure composes each release's notes from the missions finished since the last tag: finished on a later day, this mission gets a section of its own in the next release's notes, announcing the rename a second time; finished on the release day, it is left out only if the released entry already carries a heading that is exactly its title.
open-question.recommendation: The release procedure already has the rule for a finish that falls on the release day, so a section headed with the mission's exact title and a finish made directly after the release task keep the mission out of the next release's notes with no change to the release skill. If the day is missed, the cost is one duplicate section the maintainer sees and cuts at that release's pause.
open-question.alternative: Leave the release procedure's keep rule as it stands and satisfy its same-day branch: the released entry carries a section headed exactly `### Rename Cairn to Gurita`, the mission's `# ` title as it stands in requirements.md when finish reads it, and the mission is finished on the same day as the Release commit's author date, by running finish-mission directly after the release task's completion. The next release's run then counts that heading in CHANGELOG.md, finds one, and drops the finished line. Needs no change to `.claude/skills/release-plugin/SKILL.md`. It uses the rule the procedure already has for a finish that falls on the release day, so the next release leaves the mission out with no special handling. Two conditions must both hold, and if either fails the duplicate section reappears silently. The finish must land on the release's calendar day by author date, which a pause, a failed task, or crossing midnight breaks. The released entry must carry the exact title as a `###` heading, which the procedure's empty-range branch, producing `### Changes since 1.9.0`, does not give. That depends on how the entry is authored (the Release notes authoring path question) and on who runs the release and when (the Release run actor question). The mission's title must also not be revised before finish.

Change the release procedure's step 5b so the heading count it runs today only for a line dated exactly `<TAG_DATE>` runs for every kept finished line. Any finished mission whose `### <Title>` already stands as a line of CHANGELOG.md is dropped whatever its finish date. The released entry still carries `### Rename Cairn to Gurita`, and the finish may land on any later day. Removes the dependence on the calendar day. The finish can follow the release whenever the maintainer gets to it, and one small, general edit to the existing count covers any later mission that publishes as its own last task. Edits the maintainer-only release skill and still depends on the entry carrying the exact title heading, so it rests on the Release notes authoring path question as Same-day finish does. It also drops a later mission that happens to reuse an earlier release's section title, silently leaving it out of that release's notes.

Change the release procedure's step 5b to add a rule keyed on the mission's work rather than its title or date. A finished line is dropped when every commit between `<LAST_TAG>` and its finish commit that touches a path outside the mission's own directory is absent, meaning everything the mission changed was already in the tagged release, its only later commits being its own bookkeeping (the release task's completion and the finish). The released entry's headings and the finish date are left free. Independent of both the entry's headings and the calendar, so it holds however the notes for this release are authored and whenever the mission is finished. It states the actual reason the mission should be left out: its work was already released. Adds a git range read and its exact path test to a release skill that is specified step by step and has no test suite. That is the most new procedure of any option, for a case that has arisen once. A mission whose last task also touched a file outside its directory after the tag, such as a CLAUDE.md edit in the release task's completion or the finish itself, would still be kept unless the rule's exclusions are drawn exactly.

Change nothing now: neither the release procedure nor the finish's timing or title is arranged for this. The mission finishes whenever it finishes, the next release's run composes a section for it from its finish summary, and the maintainer keeps that section or removes or condenses it while reviewing that release's notes. The maintainer can do this either at the empty-range-style acceptance or by revising the committed entry during the procedure's one pause before publishing. Costs nothing in this mission and adds no rule to the release procedure for a one-time situation. The decision about the second announcement is made by the maintainer at the next release, with that release's actual notes in front of them. The next release's notes announce the rename a second time unless someone remembers to cut it. Nothing records that the cut is owed, and the next release may be months away and run by someone without this context. Trimming happens by hand inside the release's revision check, where an edit that slips outside the entry stops the run.

Reject the premise that the finish lands after the release. Publishing is taken out of the task list. The mission's last task stops before /release-plugin runs, finish-mission removes the directory under its `Mission-finish:` commit, and the release is run afterwards, so its notes are composed through the ordinary path from this mission's finished line and summary. This requires revising the Goal's "publish the result as the last task" through modify-mission-goal. The release procedure then works exactly as designed. The mission is a finished line before the tag, its summary is the source of the rename's section, and its finish date is on or before the tag date, so no later release can count it again. No rule, heading, or timing has to be arranged. Contradicts the recorded Goal, so it needs a goal revision that clears the picks it undermines. The publish then belongs to no mission's verified record, and the finish summary describes a rename that is not yet released, so a failed release leaves a finished mission claiming work that was never shipped. It also changes how the notes are authored (the Release notes authoring path question) and who runs the release and when (the Release run actor question), so it is viable only if those questions accept a release run outside the task list.

open-question.question: Where, and at what length, does the README explain the name Gurita? The naming draft holds that the name says nothing to most English speakers and that its meaning, Indonesian for octopus with the plugin as the arms that each carry a mission out on their own, should be one sentence away on the landing page. The README today explains no name: its "Why Cairn?" section is about handing long-running work to an agent, not about the word.
open-question.alternative: The root README carries one sentence on the name in the block directly under the title, beside the tagline and the pitch and above the diagram: Gurita is Indonesian for octopus, and the plugin is the arms, each carrying a mission out on its own. Nothing else in the README explains the name, the "Why" section stays about the handoff, and the host READMEs carry no explanation. It does exactly what the naming draft asks, the meaning one sentence away at the first point of contact, and the sentence doubles as a description of what the plugin does, so it costs the pitch little. It adds a third line to the densest part of the page, between title and diagram, and how it reads there depends on whether the tagline above it stays, which the README tagline question owns; a second image line next to an unchanged stone tagline would clash.

The root README glosses the name inside its opening pitch with a bare translation, a parenthetical such as "Gurita (Indonesian for octopus) brings all the important questions up…", and nothing more: no image of the arms, no section of its own, the "Why" section left about the handoff, and the three host READMEs unchanged beyond the plain rename. The cheapest possible answer to the draft's "one sentence away": the word is explained at the first place a reader meets it, with no added line on a landing page whose top is already badges, a traffic table, the title, the tagline, the pitch, and a diagram. It translates the word but drops the reason the name was chosen, the arms that each carry a mission out on their own, so the name reads as an arbitrary animal; and a "Why Gurita?" heading further down, if the section keeps that title, promises a name explanation it does not give.

The root README's "Why Cairn?" section is retitled "Why Gurita?" and opens with one sentence on the name (Indonesian for octopus, the plugin as the arms that each carry a mission out on their own), its existing paragraphs on handing long-running work to an agent following unchanged. The top of the page and the host READMEs carry no explanation. It makes the heading mean what it says, a reader asking "why this name?" finds the answer under the question, and it leads straight into the section's existing argument, since independent arms is the handoff that section describes; the top of the page stays as it is. The section sits below installation, so a reader who stops at the pitch or goes straight to the install commands never meets the meaning, which is further than the draft's "one sentence away"; and it mixes a note on the word into a section about a problem and its approach.

The root README gains a short section of its own on the name, such as "## The name", placed below the "Why" section or near the foot of the page: a paragraph saying Gurita is Indonesian and Malay for octopus, how it is pronounced (gu-RI-ta), and why the image fits, an octopus's arms each sensing and acting on their own while the head sets the goal, as a mission resolves its own questions and runs beside others. The pitch block and the "Why" section carry no explanation, and the host READMEs none. It gives the name the room to land as a design statement, carrying the pronunciation and the arms-and-head image the draft records, without touching the pitch or the handoff argument. The longest explanation stands furthest from the first mention, so the reader who most needs the gloss reaches it last or never; and a paragraph on the image is prose that ages with the design it describes and leans on the orchestrator's head that ideas/kepala.md has not yet made real.

The root README carries both: one sentence on the name in the pitch block under the title (Indonesian for octopus, the plugin as the arms that each carry a mission out), and a short paragraph further down, in its own section or opening the retitled "Why Gurita?" section, adding the pronunciation and why the image fits. The host READMEs carry no explanation. The skimming reader gets the meaning at once and the curious one the reasoning, each at the depth they want, which is the fullest answer to both "one sentence away" and the empty name explanation the README has today. The name is explained twice on one page, the paragraph partly restating the sentence, and it adds the most prose of any option to a README that is otherwise about what the plugin does; the pitch-block line also depends on the tagline's fate, which the README tagline question owns.

One sentence on the name, Indonesian for octopus with the plugin as the arms that each carry a mission out on their own, stands in the pitch block under the title of the root README and of each of the three host README templates under scripts/hosts/, rendered into every hosts/ tree and published to each distribution repository; no longer explanation anywhere. Claude Code users are pointed at the distribution repository as the recommended source, so many first meet the name on a host README rather than the root one; this puts the meaning one sentence away on every landing page a reader can arrive at. The sentence is written four times in four files that can drift apart, and the host READMEs are deliberately short distribution notes; it widens the change beyond the one README the question names, and how the host READMEs open also depends on what they say of the former name, which the former-name question owns.

No README explains the name: the root README and the host READMEs say Gurita wherever they said Cairn, the "Why" section stays about the handoff under a heading that does not ask about the word, and the meaning stays recorded only in the naming draft, ideas/gurita.md, as Cairn's meaning was never stated on the landing page. It keeps the README entirely about what the plugin does and how to install it, adds nothing to maintain, and matches how the page treated the old name, which explained no word either. It goes against the naming draft's stated intent, and the rename is exactly when readers who knew the plugin as Cairn arrive asking what the new word is; a name that says nothing to most English speakers, with no gloss anywhere a user looks, reads as arbitrary and is harder to remember and spell.
